entries.name: Upland cotton
entries.spread: Tehuacan evidence ~5500 yr BP; worldwide after the 1700s
entries.notes: The world fibre crop: 90% of global production. Lint yield above is lint only; half the seed weight is still oilseed.

entries.name: Pima (Egyptian/Sea Island) cotton
entries.spread: South America -> Caribbean -> Egypt -> global extra-long-staple after 1800s
entries.notes: The luxury staple: longest, strongest fibres. Lower yield than upland but far finer; the fibre of fine shirting.

entries.name: Flax (linseed)
entries.spread: Fertile Crescent -> Egypt, Europe, China and India by ~5000 yr BP
entries.notes: Earliest known domesticated fibre crop; linen made Egyptian wealth. French fibre yields run ~2 t/ha.

entries.name: Hemp
entries.spread: East Asia -> Central Asia and Europe by ~1000 BCE; global rope and canvas
entries.notes: Fast-growing bast fibre: 4+ t/ha fibre vs flax 2. Genome dates it to early-Neolithic East Asia.

entries.name: Jute
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Corchorus capsularis and C. olitorius
entries.spread: Indian subcontinent and Bengal delta -> global burlap trade after 1800
entries.notes: The burlap crop: second-most important natural fibre after cotton. Retting (water soaking) is mandatory to free the bast.

entries.name: Ramie
entries.spread: China -> worldwide, peaked late 19th century as 'China grass'
entries.notes: The strongest natural bast fibre; expensive to degum, so it needs blending. Known from Neolithic Chinese textiles.

entries.name: Kenaf
entries.spread: Africa and India -> tropics; substituted for jute in WWII shortages
entries.notes: Never genetically domesticated - known only in cultivation lines. Fast annual, now mostly grown for paper pulp and fodder.

entries.name: Abaca (Manila hemp)
entries.spread: Philippines -> global rope and paper trade after 1800; peaked late 1800s
entries.notes: A banana whose leaf sheaths yield 'Manila hemp', the ship-rope fibre. Perennial; harvested by hand.

entries.name: Sisal
entries.wild_ancestor: unknown agave of Chiapas/Oaxaca - a single cultivated clone
entries.spread: Mexico -> East Africa and Brazil after 1800; diesel-era rope
entries.notes: All sisal descends from one clone - genetically a single plant, spread by the Spanish. Leaf fibre for twine and rope.

entries.name: Henequen (sisal's Yucatan cousin)
entries.spread: Yucatan -> world shipping rope until synthetics, late 1800s
entries.notes: The fibre that made henequen barons: 19th-century Yucatan grew a global monopoly in binder twine. Coarse, stiff leaf fibre.

entries.name: Pineapple (pina fibre)
entries.spread: South America -> global after Columbus; fibre tradition in the Philippines
entries.notes: Philippine pina cloth (from leaf fibre) clothed the pre-Spanish nobility - translucent, stitched with piña silk blends.

entries.name: Coconut (coir fibre)
entries.spread: South India/Sri Lanka -> global matting, brushes and mattress fibre
entries.notes: The only fruit-waste fibre: husk fibre from green nuts, spun into rope that survives salt water. Byproduct of coconut palms.

entries.name: Broomcorn (broom sorghum)

domesticated.where: Ethiopia/Sudan (species); broom type later in Asia

entries.spread: East Africa -> China -> 19th-century USA 'broom corn' capital (Illinois)
entries.notes: Sorghum bred for extra-long panicles - the brush in every straw broom. Famously the crop that collapsed Ohio/Illinois broom towns when plastic bristles came.

entries.name: Sheep (wool)
entries.spread: Fertile Crescent -> worldwide by 2000 BCE
entries.notes: Woolly sheep only appear ~8000 BP; early sheep were hairy meat animals. Useful symbol of the Secondary Products Revolution.

entries.name: Angora goat (mohair)
entries.spread: Ankara -> Europe 1550s; South Africa 1838; now S Africa/Texas/Australia
entries.notes: Lustrous single-coat fibre, superb dye uptake. A single breed kept secret by the Ottomans; first described by Europeans in 1554.

entries.name: Cashmere goat (underwool)
entries.wild_ancestor: bezoar goat (Capra aegagrus) - Central Asian type
entries.spread: Central Asia -> Kashmir shawl trade; now China/Mongolia dominate
entries.notes: Only the fine underdown (~15 microns) counts as cashmere - 100-300 g per goat per year. Luxury by sheer scarcity.

entries.name: Mulberry silkworm
entries.spread: China -> Korea/Japan 1st c. CE, Byzantium 6th c., worldwide 19th c.
entries.notes: The only fully domesticated insect: cannot survive wild, lives entirely on mulberry. ~1 km of filament per cocoon.

entries.name: Eri silkworm (peace silk)
entries.spread: Assam and Northeast India -> SE Asia
entries.notes: Open-cocoon silkworm - the moth emerges, so no boiling alive ('ahimsa silk'). Wool-like, never reels, must be spun.

entries.name: Chinese oak silkworm (tussah)
entries.spread: Shandong, China -> reared worldwide, coarse 'wild silk'
entries.notes: Tussah is the 'wild silk' of fabrics - coarser, golden, tougher. Domesticated only ~400 yr ago; rearing documented from 1651.

entries.name: Alpaca
entries.spread: Andes -> global luxury fibre since the 1980s
entries.notes: Finest of the camelid fibres (~15-25 micron), softer than wool. ~2.5-4 kg fleece per head per shearing.

entries.name: Llama
entries.spread: Andes -> global (pack animal as much as fibre)
needs: pack loads on llama's back, not the alpaca's
entries.notes: The camel of the New World: pack beast with coarse outer coat. Alpaca and llama interbreed freely - hybrid 'huarizo'.

entries.name: Angora rabbit
entries.spread: Ankara -> Eastern Europe by ~600 CE, France 1723, now China leads
entries.notes: Fibre per kg of body weight unmatched among animals (~1 kg/yr). France built an industry from 1723; Marie Antoinette kept them.

entries.name: Yak (down)
entries.spread: Tibetan Plateau -> high Asia; qiviut-like down is a luxury niche
entries.notes: The high-altitude ox: ~1 kg of cashmere-grade down per head per year, plus coat for rope and tents.

entries.name: Bactrian camel (hair)
entries.spread: Central/Inner Asia along the Silk Roads -> steppe Asia
entries.notes: True camel hair: soft underdown shed in spring, combed not shorn. Coat warmth without bulk for desert cold.

entries.name: Dromedary (hair)
entries.spread: Arabia -> North Africa, Sahel, Somalia, India, Australia
entries.notes: Coarser, patchier shed than Bactrian, but the riding animal of the Arab world - wool for tents (the 'beit al sha'ar', house of hair).

entries.name: True indigo
entries.spread: India -> SE Asia, China; Caribbean/S Carolina plantations from 1600s
entries.notes: The blue of antiquity - Indus Valley indigo, Egyptian mummy cloth ~4300 BP. Fermented leaf vats -> indigotin.

entries.name: Dyer's knotweed (Japanese indigo)
entries.spread: China -> Japan by the 8th c.; centre of Awa/Tokushima dye culture
entries.notes: Japan's own indigo: textiles dyed with it date to the late 700s. Leaves composted 100 days into 'sukumo' before dyeing.

entries.name: Dyer's woad
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Isatis tinctoria (central/western Asia) - cultivated, not truly domesticated
entries.spread: Central Asia -> Iron Age Europe; medieval Languedoc/Thuringen dye fortunes
entries.notes: Europe's only blue for millennia - Caesar's Britons 'painted blue' with woad. Yield only 0.2% vs indigo's 1%; eclipsed after 1600.

entries.name: Common madder
entries.spread: Near East -> Egypt (5000 yr BP), Mediterranean, worldwide; Tutankhamun's tomb
entries.notes: The red of armies and empires - 'Turkey red' was madder's masterpiece. Yield ~3-4 t dry roots/ha after 3 years; today artisanal.

entries.name: Saffron crocus
entries.spread: Crete -> Persia, Kashmir, Spain; global spice/dye/perfume
needs: dry hot summers, cool wet winters
entries.notes: Sterile triploid - every corm is a clone; it cannot seed. ~15000 flowers per kg dried stigma (0.01 t/ha); far costlier as dye.

entries.name: Safflower
entries.spread: Fertile Crescent -> Egypt (4000 yr BP), India, China AD 300, oil worldwide
entries.notes: Red carthamin and yellow dyes from petals - Tutankhamun garlands. 'Bastard saffron' for cooks; now mostly an oil crop.

entries.name: Weld (dyer's rocket)
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Reseda luteola (Europe) - cultivated, not truly domesticated
entries.spread: Europe; the yellow of medieval tapestry and ecclesiastical cloth
entries.notes: The finest lightfast yellow of pre-synthetic times - used with woad to make green. Widely cultivated, never really domesticated.

entries.name: Turmeric
entries.spread: India -> SE Asia and China by antiquity; global spice and dye
entries.notes: The robes of Buddhist monks - curcumin dyes yellow and (with mordants) broad browns. Fresh rhizome ~20 t/ha.

entries.name: Annatto (achiote)
entries.spread: Amazonia -> Caribbean by pre-Columbian era; global food colour
entries.notes: The urucu of Amazonian body paint (bixin) - oldest annatto record is Caribbean, but domestication is Amazonian. Body-paint to margarine colour.

entries.name: Henna
entries.spread: Middle East/North Africa -> India; global body-art and hair dye
entries.notes: Egyptian mummies were stained with henna ~5000 yr BP. Lawsone concentrates in the leaf - India makes 10,000+ t of dried leaf a year.

entries.name: Cochineal (grana fina)
entries.spread: Mixteca Oaxaca -> Spain 1523; THE red of 17th-18th c. Europe
entries.notes: ~250 kg dried insects per hectare of nopal per year (three 90-day cycles). The second-most-valuable colonial Mexican export - red coats everywhere.

entries.name: Persian walnut (husk dye)
entries.spread: Central Asia -> Europe by antiquity; global nut tree
entries.notes: Husk and bark give fast brown-black (juglone); Flemish painters and dyers used it for centuries. A food tree that dyes.

entries.name: Cutch (catechu)
entries.spread: India/Myanmar -> global leather tannin and dye
entries.notes: The khaki dye: boiled acacia heartwood + iron made 'khaki' literally mean dust-coloured cloth. Also the betel-chew tannin.

entries.name: Lac insect (shellac)
entries.spread: India/SE Asia -> global shellac (varnish) and lac-dye trade
entries.notes: Farmed on host trees since antiquity - the world's only animal-derived commercial resin. Lac-dye was a major crimson before cochineal won.
